title: Default Mode Network Changes
subtitle: Self, autobiographical memory and internal narrative
altText: Chalkboard-style clinical neuroscience diagram illustrating default mode network changes across threat, memory, regulation and treatment systems.
learningObjectives: Explain default mode network changes in clinically accurate language.
Distinguish established findings from theoretical or mixed claims in default mode network changes.
Identify one limitation or safety implication relevant to default mode network changes.

sections.explainSimply: The default mode network supports self-related thought and autobiographical processing.
sections.explainLikePsychologist: Trauma-related intrusions, shame and altered self-continuity may involve disrupted coordination within and between default-mode, salience and executive networks.
sections.advancedClinicalDetail: Resting-state results vary with analysis method, state, medication and comorbidity; mechanism claims remain inferential.
sections.thinkOfItLike: Think of default mode network changes as one part of a dynamic safety-and-learning system rather than a single switch.
sections.whyPsychologistsCare: Psychologists need default mode network changes to connect symptoms with learning, context, risk and treatment choice without reducing the person to a brain scan.
sections.whenItGoesWrong: Resting connectivity does not reveal a person’s private memories.
sections.clinicalPearl: Clinical pearl: use default mode network changes to sharpen formulation, not to replace phenomenology or outcome measurement.
sections.practicalExample: A clinician uses default mode network changes to formulate triggers, state shifts, avoidance and functional impact, then monitors whether intervention improves daily life rather than relying on presumed neural change.
sections.limitationsCautions: Resting connectivity does not reveal a person’s private memories. Evidence classification: mixed network evidence.
